title: Inspiration
summary: These passages speak about Scripture in distinct ways. Deuteronomy 6:4–9 tells Israel to keep God’s words and teach them through daily life. Psalm 19 praises the Lord’s instruction as life-giving and wise, while Psalm 119 describes holding that word close as a guide for conduct. Luke 24 depicts Jesus interpreting Moses and the Prophets in relation to his suffering and glory. Second Timothy 3:14–17 says the sacred writings make a person wise for salvation and equip for good work, describing Scripture as God-breathed. Together, these passages show Scripture instructing, guiding, and bearing witness; they do not by themselves resolve every later debate about the doctrine of inspiration.
historical_context: The cited passages present several textual settings: Deuteronomy’s instruction to Israel, praise in Psalms, Luke’s account after Jesus’ resurrection, counsel to Timothy, and Hebrews’ opening contrast between prophetic speech and speech in the Son. The object’s source list supports these textual observations but does not provide an independently reviewed basis for more detailed historical reconstruction.
canonical_context: The selected texts move from Israel’s instruction and praise of God’s word to its interpretation in Luke and the description of sacred writings in 2 Timothy. They present related but distinct claims: Deuteronomy calls Israel to teach the covenant words, the Psalms praise divine instruction, Luke shows Jesus reading Israel’s Scriptures in light of his mission, and 2 Timothy emphasizes the sacred writings’ role in salvation and formation.
literary_context: The references include instruction in Deuteronomy, two poems of praise in Psalms, a resurrection narrative in Luke, a letter’s counsel to Timothy, and the opening of Hebrews. Their different forms matter: a command to teach, a song praising instruction, a narrative scene of interpretation, and a letter’s description of Scripture are not interchangeable statements. Second Timothy 3:14–17 explicitly calls the sacred writings God-breathed and describes their use; the other passages illustrate ways Scripture is taught, praised, and interpreted.
covenantal_significance: Deuteronomy 6:4–9 places God’s words within Israel’s covenant life: they are to be kept, taught to children, and recalled in ordinary routines. Second Timothy 3:14–17 speaks of sacred writings making Timothy wise for salvation and equipping him for good work. The passages connect Scripture with a formed life, while retaining their distinct settings and emphases.
canonical_role: This entry gathers passages that portray Scripture as covenant instruction, praised guidance, interpreted witness, and sacred writings that equip for good work. Its anchors support those observations; they do not settle every later doctrinal question associated with inspiration.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Inspiration in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
